title: The physician's sons (Kern ch. 15)
hook: a doctor's children take poison; he leaves word he's died so they'll take the medicine

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha said he woke ages beyond counting ago, and only seems to leave. Your line: always here. Who did you reach out to far away? Today, he explains why he seems to leave. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

Nobody in the house will touch the bottle on the counter. It's the right medicine. It's been there for days. Everybody knows it would help. And still it sits there, because it smells strange, or it tastes bitter, or because taking it would mean admitting something's wrong. Yesterday the Buddha said he only seems to pass away, and he promised a reason. Today he gives it the way the Lotus likes to give things: as a story. A doctor, a house full of children, a poison, and a medicine that sits untouched. Today: the physician's sons.
screen: `A BOTTLE ON THE COUNTER.` → `THE RIGHT MEDICINE.` → `NOBODY TOUCHES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the poison. A wise and skilled physician has many sons. He travels abroad, and while he's gone, the children get into some poison and drink it. When he comes home, they're writhing on the floor. They see him and they're overjoyed: father, you're back, help us. Second, the split. He mixes a medicine that looks good, smells good and tastes good, and gives it to them. Some of the sons, whose minds the poison hasn't reached, take it at once and are healed. The others are glad to see him, and they ask to be cured, but they won't take it. The poison has turned their minds. The medicine seems wrong to them. Third, the message. So the father makes a plan. He tells them: I'm old, and my time is near. Here's the medicine. Take it. Then he goes away again, and sends a messenger home with the news that their father has died. The sons are crushed. If he were here, they say, he'd look after us. Now we're alone. And that grief brings them back to themselves. They look at the medicine, and see that it's good. They take it. They're healed. When the father hears, he comes home, and they see him again. Fourth, the question. The Buddha asks the assembly: did that physician tell a lie? No, they say. Neither do I, says the Buddha. I seem to pass away so that people, missing me, will turn to the teaching I've left. It's the same move as the burning house and the phantom city, and this time the one using it is a father who wanted his children well more than he wanted them to see him.
screen: `THE SONS DRINK POISON.` · `SOME TAKE IT, SOME WON'T.` · `WORD COMES THAT HE HAS DIED.` · `WAS THE DOCTOR LYING?` · then, large: `TAKE THE MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: take one medicine you avoid. Settle, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind one thing you know is good for you that keeps sitting on the counter: a hard conversation, an apology, a night of real sleep, a walk, a call you keep not making. Notice what makes it seem bitter. Don't argue with that. Just see it. Then picture yourself picking it up and taking it, simply, the way the first sons did. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The physician's sons. Children who wouldn't take the cure until word came that their father was gone, and then they did. Today's word.
Your line: take the medicine. Today, take one small dose of the good thing you've been avoiding, before anyone has to leave for you to do it. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the parable of the physician and his sons is told with the chapter on the Buddha's lifespan, to explain why the Buddha appears to pass away though he is always present.

fork.setup: you're the physician. some of your children are poisoned, and they're glad you're home, but they won't take the medicine. what do you do?
options: hold them down and force it.
leave, and send word that you've died.
wait at home until they change their minds.
fork.reveal: he goes away and sends word of his death. grief brings the sons to their senses; they take the medicine, and he comes home.

original.note: Sanskrit: medicine, a remedy; the physician's gift to his sons.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange story about a dad who fakes his own death.
what it means: the Buddha seems to pass away so that people, missing him, finally take the teaching he left.
what a scholar hears: the chapter names its own skillful means and asks outright whether it's a lie; the assembly says no.

notes: Parable paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 15, not quoted (wording unverified). The number of sons given in the text is deliberately left out under the claims rule.

Check: physician abroad; sons drink poison; on return some take the medicine and are cured, others with perverted minds welcome him but refuse; he says he's old and near death, leaves the medicine, goes abroad and sends word he has died; grief brings them to their senses; they take it; he returns; the Buddha asks whether he lied.
Practice treats 'medicine' as a picture (conversation, apology, sleep) and gives no medical advice; confirm the tone.
Original: भैषज्य (bhaiṣajya), medicine; the parable's word may be agada or auṣadha. Confirm.
